To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the tumour-promoter, phorbol esters, thrombin and the peptide hormone, vasopressin, induce a differential activation and translocation of three isoforms of PKC in human platelets.

the tumour-promoter phorbol esters and physiological agonists such as thrombin and vaso- pressin induce translocation of PKCs from the cytosol to membranes in platelets, and that the translocation is different for each PKC isoform and for each agonist.

the three isoforms of protein kinase C in human platelets have different subcellular distribution and translocation kinetics after exposure to the physiological agonists thrombin and vasotocin, and that this translocation is regulated by calcium.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of protein kinase C (PK C) in the activation of human platelets.
the regulation of protein kinase C (PK-C) in platelets and its possible involvement in the mechanism of platelet aggregation.

the translocation of three different isoforms of PKC (alpha, beta and zeta) in human platelets, which is induced by the tumour-promoter phorbol 13-myristate 12-acetate (TPA) and two physiological stimuli, thrombin and arginine vasopressin (AVP).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the activation of PKC is dependent upon the presence of both Ca2+ and PMA, and that the activation of the different isoforms of PKC is differentially affected by the presence of Ca2+.
PMA-induced translocations are independent of Ca2+, whereas translocation induced by thrombin and vasoactive peptide are Ca2+-dependent.
the translocation of all PKC isoforms is Ca2+ dependent, whereas the translocation of only alpha-PKC is Ca2+ independent.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

PMA-induced translocations of all three PKC isoforms are dependent on extracellular Ca2+ and that thrombin-induced translocations of alpha- and beta-PKC and vasopressins-induced translocations of zeta-PKCs depend on intracellular Ca2+.
the translocation of the different isoforms is differentially regulated by Ca2+ mobilizing agonists and PMA.

the translocation of the three PKC isoforms in human blood platelets is regulated by Ca2+, with the translocation of beta-PKC being independent of Ca2+ and the translocation of both alpha- and zeta- isoforms requiring Ca2+.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the translocation of the three PKC isoforms is differentially regulated by PMA and physiological agonists, suggesting a differential role in the activation of platelet functions.
the translocation of beta- and alpha-PKC by thromboxane A2 and vasopressine is Ca2+ dependent.
PKC isoforms have different roles in the activation process and that these roles are different for each isoform.
